sections.content:
Topic of the 9 lectures:
Foundations and History of Management, Motivation, Decision Making, Personality &Emotion, Leadership, Diversity, Human Resource Management, External Analysis, Internal Analysis.

As an engineering student, the content of this course differs from my typical coursework. During each lecture, I've learned about theories, models, and concepts developed by scholars throughout history. Although I'm not particularly interested in this material, the course has equipped me with valuable knowledge, such as 'how to stay motivated' and 'how to establish leadership' - skills I believe will serve me well in the future.
sections.teaching:
This semester, the two instructors are Amanda and Mingyu, who are both pursuing their PhDs. I really appreciate how they deliver the course materials - it's better than many of the instructors I've had in the SENG and SSCI courses. Their teaching style keeps students engaged to the greatest extent possible. The way they speak and write, as well as their prompt email response times, exemplify the professionalism I expect from excellent instructors.

Mingyu has a more gentle demeanour, but she tends to include an excessive amount of information on her slides. In contrast, Amanda maintains a serious presence, but her explanations are concise and clear. While I may be slightly particular in my preferences, during some lectures, my friend and I have found it challenging to keep up with the sheer volume of material they cover. I believe it would be more effective if they provided students with materials to preview and prepare before the discussions in class.
sections.grading:
10% Attendance&Participation
The attendance policy for this course stipulates that students cannot miss more than 2 lectures to receive the full attendance mark. To earn the participation component of the grade, students must actively engage in class discussions. However, the calculation of the participation mark is ambiguous.

40% Group project
The grading is based on slides and presentations, with the assessment comprising identification and description of management issues (20%), analysis of cause (20%), generation and evaluation of alternative actions (40%), description of recommendation/implementation (10%), and presentation skills (10%).

50% Final exam
The final exam consists of 20 multiple-choice questions, 3 short answer questions, and 2 scenario analysis questions. Students are permitted to bring a double-sided A4 cheat sheet for the exam, but it is not sufficient to cover all the necessary details. With only 1 sample scenario analysis question provided beforehand, it was difficult for us to anticipate the exact content that would be covered in this portion of the exam. As a result, many students ended up including unnecessary information on their cheat sheets.
The MCs primarily test conceptual knowledge, so they are relatively manageable. However, the LQs are more challenging, as they often require providing multiple examples or applying theories to real-world problems, rather than just recalling information. This combination of question types and formats made it quite demanding to prepare thoroughly for the final exam.

Remark:
After the grades were released, I was pleasantly surprised by the final result. In my opinion, the grading was quite good, even though there were a few areas where I struggled. It's certain that I attended all the lectures, but I only participated in discussions around three times throughout the semester.

Our group also encountered challenges with the group project, as we ended up including an excessive amount of content, which seemed to leave everyone in the class a bit confused.

In the final exam, I didn't perform as well on the LQs, especially the last scenario analysis question. I had anticipated my overall grade would likely fall in the B range, perhaps a B or B+. However, to my pleasant surprise, I ended up earning an A in the course.
sections.workload:
Group project:
Origin descriptions: This group project offers you an opportunity to apply knowledge learned to real management issues presented in a reality television program – Undercover Boss. Each group will analyze an assigned episode of Undercover Boss. Each group will give a 15-minute PowerPoint presentation. At the end of each presentation, there will be a 5-minute question and answer session. We will have a random draw to determine the episode that each group will be responsible for (Actually we could make our choices).
For the group project, each team consisted of 5-6 members who were randomly assigned. Our group started prioritising our preferences 16 days before the presentation and worked on it for 2 weeks.The core requirements of the group project were to:
1. Identify and describe key management issues
2. Analyze the underlying causes of those issues
3. Generate and evaluate potential alternative actions
4. Develop a recommendation and implementation plan

Cheat sheet: The preparation of the cheat sheet for the final exam was also a significant amount of work, especially for someone like me who prefers handwriting. It took me over 15 hours to put together the cheat sheet.
Given the limitations on the number of pages allowed, I had to carefully review each set of lecture notes to ensure the content on the cheat sheet was as effective and efficient as possible.

It's also worth noting that I have a habit of taking my own additional notes after each lecture, as I believe I don't always grasp all the knowledge during the class itself. These post-lecture note-taking sessions typically take me another 2-3 hours per class.

This course provides students with a systematic approach to acquiring a solid foundation in the principles of management. Our journey begins with an introduction of what management is and the history of management. Then, we will explore the external environment and internal environment under which managers do their jobs. Quite literally, organizations operate by managers making decisions, thus we will next examine how managers make decisions. The rest of the course is organized around the four functions of management, namely planning (defining organizational goals and establishing strategies), organizing (structuring work activities), leading (influencing and motivating people), and controlling (monitoring and correcting organizational performance).
Course Objectives for Students
On completion of this course, you should be able to:
• Compare and contrast major schools of thought in the evolution of management theory
• Describe the external environment facing a manager, and explain its influences on the
manager’s work
• Describe an organization’s culture, and explain how this culture is formed and maintained
• Apply the rational approach of decision making, and discuss common biases in decision
making

sections.content:
As its name suggests, it is an introduction course of management, so you will expect some parts of the content to be based on common sense, such as "external factors affecting business environment" and "why do planning". Moreover, as a Year 2 business student, I had the advantage because some chapters of this course are identical to MGMT 2110. These include 4 functions of management (planning, organising, leading and controlling); bias of decision making (e.g. halo effect); motivation; leadership.
   There is a group project, where a group of 6 students watch an episode of Undercover Boss, analyse management issues exist in that particularly company, then give recommendations in a 15-minute presentation. A 5-minute Q&A follows, where your group will probably be challenged by the prof and the class.
   In both exams, there are MC questions which are mostly based on management concepts, and a few short essay questions, based on business cases (in which you need your common sense) and management concepts.
sections.teaching:

sections.content: Basic business concepts related to everyday life are taught. Students with advanced business background might find some concepts overlap with other business courses (e.g. unbounded rationality, red queen effect, black swan event, merger and acquisition, etc). sections.teaching:
There were three instructors for this course -- John Jamison, Arden Leung, and Andy Yun.

John Jamison was responsible for the first half of the course. He is a difficult and creative thinker who always encourages us to think deeply and independently by asking some creative questions, which are worth pondering over. Even if you sit remain silent, not voicing out your opinions, you can still gain a lot listening to him and other classmates.

Arden Leung was one of the instructors who taught the second half. Comparatively, his lessons were less interesting. Yet, his presentations and explanations were clear, illustrated with numerous daily-life examples. Despite being informative, his lessons are of high quality.

Andy Yun was a Korean lecturer who gave the last few lessons. His Korean accent and not-proficient-enough English often hindered you from understanding. His presentation was not well-organised rather. Although he is knowledgeable and experienced in management field, his teaching is not most effective IMO (yet not disastrous at least).
